questions.note: Computed load factor (12/16=0.75) correctly and correctly identified that load factor alone does not indicate trouble without knowing the collision-resolution strategy.
Correctly explained chaining: collision extends the bucket's chain, insertion stays O(1) since it never searches before writing, lookup slows in proportion to chain length (tracks load factor).

Initial claim that open-addressing lookups 'remain low until all buckets are full' was incorrect — corrected via a concrete linear-probing counterexample (3 keys colliding into slots 0,1,2) showing lookup retraces the identical probe sequence used at insertion, so read and write costs are tied together, not independent. Also corrected the framing that open addressing has a hard one-key-per-slot capacity ceiling (forces resize before load factor reaches 1.0), unlike chaining's unbounded buckets.

After the correction, independently reasoned that open addressing insertion degrades faster than chaining at the same load factor due to primary clustering (occupied slots bunching into runs that swallow more of the new arrivals), and correctly noted chaining insertion stays O(1) regardless. Needed one explicit nudge to extend this same reasoning to lookups (since lookup and insertion share the identical probe walk in open addressing, lookup must degrade by the same mechanism and magnitude) rather than treating lookup as requiring separate new math.

concepts_written: The chaining-degrades-more-gracefully claim implicitly assumes simple uniform hashing (each key equally likely to land in any bucket, independent of others) — stated explicitly after Craig questioned it

Under that assumption chain lengths cluster tightly around the load factor (Poisson-ish), so long chains are rare in practice — but chaining has no structural cap on chain length: a bad or adversarial hash function (hash-flooding attacks) can put all n keys in one bucket, giving O(n) worst-case lookup

Open addressing has a structural cap chaining lacks: since each slot holds exactly one key, no lookup can ever need more than m probes (table size) — worst case is bounded regardless of hash function quality

Net correction: 'open addressing degrades faster than chaining at the same load factor' is an average-case claim conditioned on a reasonable hash function, not a worst-case guarantee — worst-case the ranking flips, since chaining's downside is unbounded (can exceed table size m) and open addressing's is not
payload.note: Immediate follow-up to quiz_answered event 73 in the same session. Craig pushed back on the average-case open-addressing-degrades-faster claim: what stops one chaining bucket from holding dozens of keys, which could make chaining lookup worse than open addressing's? This correctly identified an unstated assumption (uniform hashing) underlying the whole prior comparison. Walked through why the assumption usually holds in practice (Poisson-distributed chain lengths at a given load factor), then conceded the real point: chaining has no structural bound on chain length (vulnerable to bad hash functions / hash-flooding attacks, unbounded by table size m), while open addressing lookup is structurally capped at m probes regardless of hash quality — so the earlier ranking is an average-case-under-uniform-hashing statement, not a worst-case one, and worst-case the ranking actually reverses. Good example of Craig catching an implicit assumption rather than accepting the stated conclusion at face value.

concepts_written: Dynamic array amortized doubling — why append is "amortized O(1)" despite occasional O(n) resize-copies
Fixed-increment growth (+k) produces resize copy-costs as an arithmetic sequence, summing to ~n^2/(2k) over n appends — average cost per append grows without bound as n grows (O(n), not O(1))
Doubling growth produces resize copy-costs as a geometric sequence, summing to ~2n over n appends — average cost per append settles at a constant regardless of n (true amortized O(1))

Worked both growth strategies by hand over 16 appends (step-by-step tables) to ground the asymptotic claim in concrete arithmetic, then projected to n=64 to show the fixed-increment average climbing while doubling stayed flat
Flagged open gap: general fact that a geometric series with any ratio > 1 sums to a bounded multiple of its largest term (needed to justify that x1.5 growth generalizes the same way) — not yet taught

concepts_written: Constant factors are dropped in Big-O -- O(log2 n) and O(log10 n) are the same class, differing only by a constant multiplier; convention uses base 2 because most log-time algorithms work by repeated halving
The halving mechanism: log_b(n) counts halvings, not items, so doubling n costs exactly one more step in log time versus n/2 more steps in linear time -- the actual mechanical reason logs are cheap
Best/worst/average case are a separate axis from growth-rate class; any of O(1)/O(log n)/O(n)/O(n^2) can carry any of the three
Unspecified Big-O defaults to worst case by convention, since it is the only guarantee that does not depend on assumptions about input distribution -- corrected from an initial average-case guess

questions.note: Asked whether merge sort's O(n log n) is uniform cost. Correctly and independently identified it as uniform in best, worst, and average case: splits are always down the middle (log n levels), and comparison work at each level is always proportional to n.

Asked to place quicksort's O(n log n) vs O(n^2) split using the worst/average-case framing from the prior session. Correctly identified the mechanism: a badly-chosen pivot against an imbalanced structure produces ~n operations per level across n levels (O(n^2) worst case), while a well-chosen pivot keeps it O(n log n) (average and best case).

Same answer went on to guess quicksort's O(n^2) worst case should be called "amortized," reasoning it describes a spiky, unpredictable cost. Genuine misconception: amortized analysis smooths a skewed sequence of many operations, not variation in a single run's cost depending on input. Quicksort's worst case is best/worst/average-case variation within one sort call, not amortized smoothing. Corrected using the uniform-vs-skewed-sequence tell from the tree-build example.

concepts_written: O(n log n) as uniform-cost: n operations each independently costing O(log n), worked via a balanced-tree build (n inserts, i-th insert costs ~log2(i)), table totaled by hand for n=8 and projected to n=64

Why the tree-build case is NOT amortized analysis: amortized analysis smooths a skewed sequence (rare expensive ops, many cheap ones); the tree build has no skew, every insert costs the same O(log n)

Merge sort use cases: guaranteed worst-case bound, stability, sequential access (linked lists, external sorting), O(n) extra space

concepts_written: Node structure (data + next pointer) and why nodes can be scattered anywhere in memory rather than adjacent
Pointer vs. reference distinction (address-holding, reassignable, no arithmetic vs. alias) -- clarified since Craig could describe the concept but not name the distinction
